extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of history of mathematics and classics
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory survey of the origins, classification, pedagogy, and branches of mathematics in ancient Greece, explaining what was considered 'mathematical', how subjects were ordered, and how they were taught. Suitable for readers studying the development of Greek mathematical thought and its social/intellectual context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions favouring scientific inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Science arises where there is leisure, organized continuity of tradition (e.g. priestly castes), and favourable environment such as colonization and wide commercial contacts (Ionian settlements in Asia Minor had contact with Egypt and Babylon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ionian Greeks benefited from commerce and contact with Babylonian and Egyptian civilizations; priesthoods in Egypt and Babylon provided industry and continuity that made early science possible but could also fossilize doctrines into dogma. The Greeks' lack of an organized priesthood allowed freer development and independent improvement of earlier knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek eclectic assimilation and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Greeks practiced 'unerring eclecticism' — they adopted serious scientific elements from Eastern traditions while discarding the 'fantastic rubbish', improving borrowed knowledge 'to fuller perfection'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and exemplars: the Epinomis' axiom 'whatever the Greeks take from the barbarians, they bring it to fuller perfection.' This principle explains Greek development of mathematical theories based on earlier observations but pursued critically and independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: No necessary opposition between religion and scientific inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek thought maintained that studying divine or 'things divine' was compatible with scientific pursuit; religious belief did not prohibit scientific study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual support: passages (Epinomis, Plato) argue God would not resent humans learning number and counting; hence inquiry into nature and divine matters is not impious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for calling a subject 'mathematical' (usage of 'mathematika')
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripatetics: subjects termed mathematika are those that cannot be known without instruction — they require a course of instruction rather than being grasped by casual acquaintance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato used 'mathema' generally for subjects of study, but the special technical use (mathematika) seems to have crystallized by Aristotle's time and in the Pythagorean school; this is why arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy were singled out as mathematika.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pythagorean quadrivium classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pythagorean list of mathematical subjects: geometry, arithmetic, astronomy (sphaeric), and music (harmonics) as closely related 'sisters'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archytas and other sources list these four subjects (order varies). Rationale: arithmetic and music concern number; geometry and sphaeric concern magnitude (plane vs magnitude in motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plato's curriculum ordering of mathematical subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Plato's educational sequence: arithmetic, geometry, stereometry (solid geometry), astronomy, harmonics — with stereometry inserted to bridge plane geometry and astronomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's reasons: logical progression (need to treat solids before motions of solids) and pedagogical emphasis (stereometry had been insufficiently studied). He also ties harmonics to astronomy by analogy of harmonious motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between arithmetic (theory) and logistic (practical calculation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic (in Plato's sense) is the theory of numbers considered in themselves (number in the abstract); logistic is the art of calculation and treating 'numbered things' (numbers as applied to objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistic comprises elementary operations, handling fractions, concrete word-problems (apples, bowls, flocks), and algorithmic methods (Greek and Egyptian multiplication/division methods). Diophantus' Arithmetica belongs conceptually to logistic despite its title because many problems originate from concrete-number contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and methods of logistic
rubrics_metrics.description: Logistic includes addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, fractions, problem-solving for concrete objects, and methods for decompositions and multiplications; branches include specific Greek/Egyptian techniques and problems like indeterminate equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: arithmetical epigrams (division of apples, weights of bowls), the cattle-problem (requiring Pell-type equations), and problems akin to Diophantus' indeterminate analysis. Logistic often deals with solving simultaneous linear equations and practical computational techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological feature: number-theory via geometrical proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Until late antiquity, number theory was largely treated in connection with geometry, using geometrical forms of proof (dots, gnomons, lines) rather than purely algebraic methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: early Pythagorean proofs using dot-figures, Euclid's Books VII–IX, Nicomachus' partial retention of geometrical reasoning, and Diophantus' fragmentary links to geometric methods in polygonal numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of geodesy (mensuration) from geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Geodesy (geodaesia) is a distinct practical subject concerned with the measurement of surfaces and volumes (mensuration), not abstract geometry of ideal figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geminus and Aristotle note geodesy measures heaps as cones and tanks/pits as cylinders — it treats tangible heaps/containers as models rather than ideal solids per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applied mathematical branches and their dependence on pure mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Applied branches (optics, mechanics, harmonics, astronomy, etc.) are dependent on pure mathematical subjects for their proofs: optics on geometry, mechanics on geometry/stereometry, harmonics on arithmetic, and phenomena on observational astronomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's mapping: proofs in applied subjects rely on pure theory; 'Phaenomena' (observational astronomy) depends on theoretical astronomy. This establishes a hierarchy where pure math underpins applied investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geminus' six-fold classification of applied mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: After arithmetic and geometry, Geminus lists six subjects concerned with sensibles: mechanics, astronomy, optics, geodesy, canonic (theory of musical intervals), and logistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order may vary in other sources (Anatolius gives logistic first). Each term is given a functional definition (e.g. canonic = division of the musical canon, geodesy = mensuration, logistic = practical calculation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of optics into three branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Optics is divided into (1) Optics proper (why things appear different in size/shape from various positions), (2) Catoptrics (theory of mirrors), and (3) Scene-painting (applied perspective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Euclid's Optics (propositions on apparent shapes/sizes), Heron's Catoptrica (angles of incidence/reflection), and applied perspective used in theatre/painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics comprises (1) construction of engines of war, (2) construction of wondrous/automatic machines, (3) mechanics proper (centres of gravity, equilibrium, mechanical powers), and (4) sphere-making (models/orreries imitating heavenly motions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Heron's automata and pneumatics, Archimedes' reputed war engines and orrery. Mechanics includes both practical machine-building and theoretical study of equilibrium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of astronomy (practical arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Astronomy includes (1) gnomonics (art of the gnomon/sundials), (2) measurement-type practices (e.g. measuring heights at which stars cross the meridian), and (3) use of dioptra for determining relative positions of celestial bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geminus' tripartition ties astronomical practice to instruments and measurement methods (Vitruvius' enumerations of sundials as context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics in Greek education: stages and subject allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary education (up to ~14): letters, music, gymnastics, and practical arithmetic (weights/measures, counting). Secondary education (~14–18): geometry and astronomy. Advanced study: deeper mathematical specialisation for a few.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato, Isocrates, and other sources indicate ages and roles: arithmetic taught with letters and games, geometry/astronomy as training for higher learning or preparation for statesmanship, and cautionary notes that deep specialization can make one 'unpractical'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical methods: use of games and concrete problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching methods emphasised amusement and practical problems (distributions of apples or garlands, games with knucklebones, bowls with mixed coins) to make arithmetic attractive and useful, connecting play with essential operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato recommends boy-suitable calculations and games to train for military logistics, household management, and sharpen attention. Examples include drawing lots with byes, distribution problems, and practical measurement exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalization and transmission of mathematical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics was taught by a range of practitioners — Pythagoreans, Sophists, itinerant teachers, and specialized masters (e.g. Hippocrates of Chios, Theodorus). Some taught for pay and professional survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes: a Pythagorean taught geometry for money after losing property; Hippocrates taught and wrote Elements; Sophists included arithmetic/geometry/astronomy among lecture subjects. The classroom interaction (Theaetetus, Theodorus) shows lectures and advanced pupil discussion.
